newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds slip back in firm two-way trade.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds slip back in firm two-way trade.

text.p: Irish bond prices slipped back in afternoon trade in line with other European bond markets although dealers said they were seeing good two-way flow as the bonds maintained their spread convergence against Germany.

"Irish bonds opened strongly this morning, narrowing by four basis points against Germany, ahead of the auction of 2006 stock," a dealer said. "Since then we've come back a bit but Irish bonds are still outperforming by two to three basis points, and we're seeing good interest from both domestics and non-residents."
By 1510 GMT, the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was down 15 pence at 102.10 to yield 5.92 percent, while the eight percent bond due 2006 was down 15 pence at 109.80 to yield 6.54 percent.
Yields against German Bunds narrowed to 153 basis points over in the five-year bond, and 81 over in the 10-year.
Ireland's National Treasury Management Agency (NTMA) on Tuesday said an 80 million punt auction of the eight percent bond due 2006 was covered 1.50 times.
"This wasn't as successful as anticipated," a dealer said. "Perhaps investors considered the bonds too expensive."
The NTMA said the highest accepted price was 110.25 for an annual yield of 6.48 percent.
The lowest accepted price and yield was 110.00 and 6.51 percent and the average price/yield was 110.08 and 6.50 percent, the NTMA said.

With the Amsterdam summit of European Union leaders drawing to a close on Tuesday, bond investors will continue to analyse Monday's deal on a stability pact, aimed at punishing countries involved in a single currency who run high budget deficits, but now with a job-creation aspect added as well.
Dealers said that EMU -- "especially a watered-down version" -- while negative for bunds, could benefit peripheral markets such as Ireland.
Looking ahead, dealers said, the Irish backdrop was supportive of bonds.

"The underlying tone of the currency remains firm, and inflation is subdued," a dealer said. "Also in July there's a redemption of one billion Irish pounds of the 1997 bond which will mean a lot of cash for re-investment."
The resultant supply and demand mismatch would support bond prices, he added.
Earlier, the U.S. consumer price index, showed that inflationary pressure was almost entirely absent from the U.S. economy.
In the UK, the main number of the week is retail sales tomorrow, with analysts forecasting a rise in May against April of 0.3 percent.
